schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the wording ('Now'='And', 'slept'='lay down'), noting the verse is literally the same as 1 Kings 22:50; Keil explains the death-notice opens ch. 21 because Joram's fratricide connects to it, and flags the material peculiar to the chronicler.
Gill glosses the idiom briefly: Jehoshaphat died as his fathers died.
Henry frames the chapter as the tragedy of an indulgent father and a fratricidal son.
Clarke lays out the whole arc of the reign in a single summary.

themes: a good father and a wicked son

schools.summary: Keil names the six brothers and reads the verse as the setup for their murder, doubting avarice was the motive and preferring their disapproval of the idolatrous course.
Clarke calls 'king of Israel' a scribal corruption for 'Judah' (versions + 38 MSS); Wesley defends it as meaningful — Jehoshaphat reigned by right and over many settled Israelites.
Gill notes only that these were Jehoshaphat's sons whom Jehoram succeeded.

debates.question: Is 'Jehoshaphat king of Israel' a scribal error?

sides.position: A corruption for 'king of Judah,' to be restored from the versions and manuscripts
A meaningful title — Jehoshaphat reigned by right and over many Israelites settled in his kingdom

schools.summary: Gill likens the gifts to Abraham's dismissal of his concubines' sons with presents from Isaac.
Keil itemizes the endowment — silver, gold, precious things, fenced cities — the crown alone going undivided to the firstborn.
Henry admires the father's fairness but questions preferring an unfit firstborn: the birthright gave only a double portion (Deut. 21:17), and the people's security is the supreme law.
Clarke reads the chronology in 'kingdom': a co-regency of about three years, so Jehoram reigned only some five years after his father's death.
Gill notes Jehoram now 'reigned alone,' having shared the throne with his father.
Keil marks 'strengthened himself' (as at 2 Chron. 1:1) and judges the brothers slain for disapproving the idolatry, not from greed.

Wesley reads 'strengthened himself' as 'hardened his heart' and identifies the princes as godly northern refugees; Clarke calls the lust of power diabolic, noting such fratricide is common among bad Asiatic kings.
Henry reads Jehoram's motive as Cain's — he slew his brethren because their piety condemned his impiety — and pronounces the woe of Hab. 2:12.
Keil marks the verse as the head of the reign's record, where the account rejoins 2 Kings 8:17-22; Ellicott notes the chronicler names Jehoram again where Kings has only 'he was.'
Gill treats the verse as matter already handled and defers to the parallel.

Ellicott marks the emphatic 'he made' against Asa and Jehoshaphat (2 Chron. 17:6), the point where the narrative becomes peculiar to the chronicler, the 'mountains/cities' variant, and 'compelled' = 'seduced' (Deut. 13:6).
Gill: the high places were idol-shrines rebuilt where Asa and Jehoshaphat had torn them down.
Clarke reads 'fornication' as the spiritual adultery of idolatry — Israel wedded to Jehovah; Wesley: the king compelled the people by force, threats, and penalties.
Henry: Jehoram seduced Jerusalem and compelled the country, using for the church's destruction the power given for its edification (Rev. 2:20).

themes: narrative now peculiar to the chronicler

schools.summary: Gill: Elijah wrote it before his translation, foreseeing Jehoram's crimes, and left it (with Elisha, per Kimchi) to be delivered at the proper time.
Henry: the difficulty is one of order — the translation-story stands out of place; Elijah, near departure, left the writing to be sent, and Jehoram threw it by as waste-paper.

Wesley agrees Jehoram reigned before the translation; Clarke canvasses every theory, rejects Kennicott's 'Elisha' (all MSS/versions read Elijah), and inclines to a prophecy uttered in Elijah's lifetime, now laid before the king.
Ellicott offers both a still-living Elijah (extreme age explaining a written warning) and a posthumous document of his last utterances forwarded by a pupil.

debates.question: How could a writing come from Elijah, who seems already translated before Jehoram's reign?

sides.position: Elijah was still alive; the account of his translation stands out of chronological order
Elijah composed it before his translation and left it (with Elisha) to be delivered at the appointed time

themes: 'the LORD God of David thy father'

schools.summary: Gill: to walk in the way of the kings of Israel was to worship the calves and Baal.
Ellicott fixes the verb 'go a whoring' (as at v.11; the rare zanah of 1 Chron. 5:25) and ties 'slain thy brethren' to v.4; Keil binds the charge to the coming penalties.
Henry lays out the letter as a charge-sheet: apostasy, conformity to Ahab, enforced idolatry, and the murder of better men.

Ellicott renders 'smite a great smiting,' its object unexpressed — Jehoram struck in people, sons, wives, and goods by the Philistine-Arab invasion; Keil takes it as the first, outward stroke of the two-fold doom.
Clarke gives the Targum's 'the Word of the LORD will send a great mortality.'
Gill: the people, willing sharers in the idolatry, deserved the blow, which was itself a punishment to the king.
Henry: bad men bring judgments on all about them — people for complying, wives for seducing him.
Gill: the disease of the bowels was a just retaliation on a man who showed no bowels of compassion to his brethren.
Henry contrasts Asa (diseased in the feet) with Jehoram (struck in the inwards), and notes the mercy of a warning given beforehand.
Ellicott renders the doubled Hebrew (cf. Deut. 28:59; Prov. 18:14) and reads 'day by day' as 'a year upon a year,' i.e. two years (cf. v.19).
Clarke sets Jehoram among the tyrants (Antiochus Epiphanes, Herod Agrippa) who died of the bowels; Wesley marks the blood-for-blood justice on people and wives.

outliers.note: Sets Jehoram among the tyrants — Antiochus Epiphanes and Herod Agrippa — who perished of the same disease of the bowels.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains 'stirred up the spirit' (Jer. 51:11; Hag. 1:14; cf. Isa. 13:17), pairs Philistines and Arabians as Judah's enemies, ties the raid to Joel 3:4-6, and locates the Cushites in southern Arabia; Keil reads the invasion as the outward blow of v.14 falling.
Gill marks the reversal: Philistines who paid Jehoshaphat tribute now invade his apostate son.
Wesley: God raised the spirits of a subdued people to do his work; Clarke: no other account survives of this ruinous predatory war — a general curse on body, soul, substance, family, and government.

Ellicott renders 'clave it asunder' (Exod. 14:16), infers the enemy entered Jerusalem (concise, like the Shishak notice, 2 Chron. 12:9), and reads Jehoahaz/Ahaziah as one name ('Iah holdeth'), judging 'Azariah' a mistake.
Henry: the raiders struck the king's house only — the controversy was with Jehoram — and blood-for-blood, all his sons slain but one.
Wesley: the wives slain too (save Ahaziah and Athaliah), the one son spared only as of David's house, for the blessing of the Messiah; Clarke gives the survivor three names.
Gill notes the hostile incursion into Judah.

debates.question: Is 'Azariah' (2 Chron. 22:6) a genuine third name of the surviving son or a scribal error?

sides.position: A genuine third name, alongside Jehoahaz and Ahaziah
A scribal mistake for Ahaziah, which the versions read

themes: one heir spared for the covenant

schools.summary: Keil marks the turn from the outward blow to the inward, upon the king's own body; Ellicott fixes 'incurable' (lit. 'to want of healing,' cf. 2 Chron. 36:16) and notes the Syriac/Arabic bind vv.16-18 into one prophecy.
Gill weighs the physicians' guesses and settles on a dysentery or bloody flux (Targum: 'the Word of the LORD broke him').
Henry pictures the grievous, tedious two-year sickness, adding that to good men such diseases are fatherly chastisements, to Jehoram unmixed judgment.
Ellicott fixes the two-year term, exactly coinciding with the prediction; Keil wrestles the difficult Hebrew of the time-phrase and the death 'in sore pains'; both mark the withheld burning.
Gill notes the two years' torment before death.
Clarke: no burning of aromatic woods as for his forefathers (cf. 2 Chron. 16:14); the Targum's constipation and inflammation ending in the bowels' gushing out.
Henry: the king's memory so unloved that they denied his loathsome corpse even the customary spices.

Keil and Ellicott explain the repeated regnal figures as drawn from a special source, render 'departed without being desired' as 'died unregretted/mourned by none' (correcting Luther's 'walked not rightly'), and read the burial apart from the kings as a further dishonour (cf. 2 Chron. 24:25; 26:23).
Clarke: hated living and neglected dead, cursed of God, with no annalist to record his life — the rock on which he wrecked the state.
Henry: unvalued and unlamented, denied the royal tombs, his exclusion a figure of the everlasting separation of the wicked.

debates.question: Are the chronicler's additions to Jehoram's history reliable?

sides.position: Historical, drawn from a special source with its own peculiar language
Partly legendary, with pure embellishment by the chronicler

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the verse repeats 2 Kings 8:18 word for word; Keil sets the sin against the mercy of the next verse and heads the section on the revolts.
Clarke names the wife Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, likely the principal cause of Jehoram's cruelty and profaneness.
Henry unfolds the wreckage: Jehoram made high places and set up idolatry again, ruining the reformation of his father and grandfather.

themes: marriage into the house of Ahab

schools.summary: Keil notes the chronicler recasts the parallel — the house of David spared for the covenant's sake, the lamp promised 'to his sons'; Ellicott defends the expansion, weighing 'covenant for David' (Isa. 55:3, cf. Josh. 9:6) and rendering 'lamp.'
Clarke glosses the light as 'a descendant,' an unbroken line on David's throne.
Henry grounds the sparing in the covenant of Ps. 89:30 — David's seed scourged but the covenant unbroken — because the blessing in it is the Messiah.
Ellicott sets the revolt against 2 Kings 8:20 and recalls that under Jehoshaphat only a deputy ruled Edom (1 Kings 22:47); Keil binds it to the moral cause stated at v.10.
Clarke refers the reader to the fuller account at 2 Kings 8:21.
Henry draws the rule: when Jehoram cast off his allegiance to God, his subjects cast off their allegiance to him.

themes: Edom once ruled by a deputy

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the night sortie not as a victory but as Jehoram's desperate escape, cutting through the encircling Edomites, and mends Kings' 'Zair' to 'Seir'; Keil confirms the failure from the parallel's 'the people fled to their tents.'

outliers.note: Against the surface reading, insists the verse records no triumph but a breakout from encirclement; the campaign to recover Edom failed.

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes 'unto this day,' the seam with 2 Kings 8:22, and the chronicler's added moral ground (the Tyrian Baal to please Athaliah), rejecting the readings of Thenius and Hitzig; Keil binds the revolts to the same stated cause.
Wesley: Libnah set up a free state — while Jehoram adhered to God they adhered to him, but when he cast God off, they cast him off.
Henry notes Libnah's old royalty (Josh. 12:15) and that its revolt, whatever its justification, justifies God's providence.

debates.question: Why did Libnah revolt from Jehoram?

sides.position: Because Jehoram had forsaken the LORD (the chronicler's own stated cause)
Because Libnah, a priestly city, refused obedience to an idolatrous king
